title: Maclaurin series
objectives: Derive a Maclaurin series from the derivatives of a function at x = 0.
Recall and use the standard series for eˣ, sin x, cos x and ln(1 + x).
Explain what the interval of convergence means, and see it on a graph.
Use series to approximate values and evaluate limits.

explanation.heading: Matching derivatives at zero
body: Suppose a function can be written as a polynomial that never ends:
Putting x = 0 gives a₀ = f(0). Differentiate once and put x = 0 again: a₁ = f′(0). Differentiate twice: 2a₂ = f″(0). In general the n-th derivative picks out n! × aₙ, so
The factorial is the part students most often forget. It comes from repeatedly differentiating xⁿ: n × (n − 1) × … × 1.

explanation.heading: The standard series
body: sin x = x − x³/3! + x⁵/5! − … (all x)
ln(1 + x) = x − x²/2 + x³/3 − … (−1 < x ≤ 1)
sin x is odd, so only odd powers appear; cos x is even, so only even powers. Other series come from these by substitution (replace x by 2x, or by x²) or by multiplying two series together.

explanation.heading: Why more terms help, and where they stop helping
body: Near x = 0, each extra term corrects the error left by the one before. Far from 0, the highest power in your polynomial dominates and the approximation shoots off.

For eˣ, sin x and cos x the series converges for every x. You just need more terms the further out you go. For ln(1 + x), no number of terms works once |x| > 1: that is what a finite interval of convergence means.

demo.intro: The gray curve is sin x. Step up the number of terms and watch the polynomial approximation grip more of it.
notice: Each new term roughly extends the region of good agreement by π in each direction.
Outside that region the polynomial diverges violently, up or down depending on the sign of the last term.
With one term the approximation is just y = x: the small-angle approximation sin x ≈ x.

examples.title: Substitution
examples.problem: Find the Maclaurin series for e<sup>2x</sup> up to the term in x³.

steps.do: Start from eᵘ = 1 + u + u²/2 + u³/6 + …
steps.why: Use the known series rather than differentiating again.
The x terms cancel, leaving the x³ term in front.
Every later term still has a positive power of x.

takeaways: aₙ = f⁽ⁿ⁾(0) / n!. Never forget the factorial.
Build new series by substitution or multiplication instead of differentiating from scratch.
An approximation is only trustworthy near 0, and only inside the interval of convergence.
